utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please be so kind as to call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, welcome in the courtroom again. The Chamber is glad to see that you recovered, at least recovered sufficiently to appear in court again during this week. So welcome, and we wish you -- if there's any need for further recovery, we wish you all the best to that. We have on our agenda for today a number of items. Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, first of all, thank you for giving me the floor. But before we really begin to deal with our agenda, I would like to ask your permission not to speak -- not to speak for 30 minutes and to not speak on my feet because I believe it is the duty of all lawyers in international law. Because at one point one should know how to assume one's duties. And if you allow me, I will remain silent for 30 seconds. This is the Defence's way of showing our tacit protest before the International Tribunal of the United Nations, protest against what is happening to other people, namely the violation of international law and the fundamental principles in which we and the International Community believe. I therefore ask your permission to remain silent on my feet for 30 seconds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber emphasises that everyone is free to express his view on what happens at this moment in the world. At the same time, the Chamber of course cannot prohibit you from being silent and to express yourself in this courtroom. On the other hand, the Chamber feels that this matter is not part of this case and we should separate. Therefore, the Chamber will not give you any permission to do or not do what you ask us. The Chamber considers this a matter which is not to be dealt with at this moment in this court. At the same time, the Chamber supports fully the freedom of expression which does not necessarily mean that at every place one should express its view on that. So therefore, we'll neither give you permission nor are we specifically prohibiting. It's not relevant for this case. Therefore, no decision will be taken on your request.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. May I ask you perhaps more diplomatically to be patient to bear with me for 30 seconds before we begin with our work according to our agenda?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. It's -- it has got nothing to do with this case. And therefore, as I told you before, the Chamber is aware that people may have strong feelings, may have strong opinions about it, they should be free to express themselves about it, but it's not a matter that should be considered in whatever way, in a negative way or a positive way, in this case in this court. Therefore, we just will proceed with the agenda. On our agenda at this moment is -- let me just have a look -- rebuttal evidence, exhibits that are still outstanding on which no decision has been taken, and some of them we still are waiting for a point of view of one of the parties or both parties. One specific exhibit in this respect is the video material that has been tendered recently with three sequences, video material pointed at as coming from the fifth tape, as we call it. And then we have still - that's also part of the outstanding exhibits - specifically the documents related to the testimony of the military expert, where some documents were tendered from the bar table where the Prosecution has expressed itself in a -- in the Radinovic statements, which has been disclosed to the Defence. So I'd first like to go to the rebuttal evidence. The Chamber has received the response from the Defence that was filed yesterday in relation to the rebuttal evidence. May I first ask the Defence whether the Chamber can consider this to be the response, or is there anything that should be added to your written response?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. There will doubtlessly be something to add.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if there's specific points you'd like to add, you can do it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps we could come back to it later. Certain things are very clearly expressed in this document. We don't know whether the Prosecution holds its position still, because in their submission there are certain things that appear to us obviously inadmissible, and perhaps we can make an effort, if the Prosecution tells us that they continue to stand by this position, we could perhaps ask them to clarify whether this is so and if we are perhaps to withdraw some of the elements that we quoted in our submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ierace, you have read, I take it, the response of the Defence? There is on -- on almost all of the 92 bis statements is an objection. Do I understand you well, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, Ms. Pilipovic, that your response also covers the viva voce witnesses? Because it says Defence response on Prosecution motion pursuant to Rule 92 bis in relation to rebuttal. Could you please clarify the position of -- it's about Mr. From. I take it that the viva voce witnesses are covered fully or ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. But what I would like to say is that I wrote a letter to the Prosecution in one of the languages of the Tribunal, as I'm required, and I still didn't get an answer. One of the things I asked is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, may I -- did you want to say that you wrote it in French or did you want to --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you wrote it in French, that's clear. It gives also a clue as to why there might not be an immediate answer. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because -- because, of course, I can say French. Anyway, I didn't get an answer either in English or in French. I asked the question very clearly; namely, since when this famous logistician was available.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Softwares, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps we'll hear from that, if we give an opportunity to the Prosecution to respond. Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I assume my learned colleague is referring to a letter that the Prosecution received this morning in French. And indeed we were able to have it translated reasonably promptly. I've now known its contents for some two and a half hours. And as I understand it, whereas the Prosecution had offered the Defence yesterday, had renewed its offer to the Defence yesterday to attend a demonstration of Mr. From's software, the essence of the response this morning was to decline the invitation. So I don't know how that correspondence impacts on the remaining issues before the Trial Chamber this afternoon. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Mr. Ierace, could you please respond, then, to the submissions made by the Defence in response of your -- of the rebuttal evidence you have applied for -- at least you have applied for leave to present this rebuttal evidence. And I would specifically ask your attention for one issue, where it seems that the photograph and the testimony of Mr. Babic seems to be related to the structure of the school of theology, especially in respect of the number of storeys that existed during the war. It seems from the answer that it's not the Prosecution's case that there -- not the Defence case that there was one story added after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I noticed that. The evidence of the relevant witness was that an upper floor of one of the buildings was damaged and he identified the floor as being a third floor of a particular building and he said that it was thus unsafe to travel onto that floor. So that extent, I agree with the Defence. However, the witness went on to say a few pages later that the building, both during the war and pre-war, did not have a fourth floor, that the fourth floor only existed for the first time post-war. And the evidence of the Prosecution witness to be called in rebuttal clearly refutes that. It makes clear that there was a four-storey building in the complex pre-war and that that floor was intact at the end of the conflict and following renovations it continues to have a fourth floor. So that's the direct relevance of it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The -- Mr. Piletta-Zanin, one of your witnesses, Witness DP4, said -- I'll just take one line out of his testimony, that -- about the school of theology. "So before the war and during the war this part here was only composed of only three storeys, so it was only a three-storey building at that time," which suggests that one floor was added. It does not only suggest it, but since in a previous line he says "it was just right after the war because the convent was so damaged, one floor was added after the war." I now understand from your response that it's not the Defence case that the -- one floor was added to the building after the war. Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will check this with Mrs. Pilipovic because I didn't quite understand it now. But anyway, I just asked a very precise question of the Prosecution and I didn't get an answer. I wanted to know when this software became available, not only to the public but in specialised agencies, and I wanted this to be made available to us. The Prosecution cannot make a demonstration for us if they don't have basic information, and this is not the first time this is happening. As far as the number of floors is concerned, we will look into it and get you an answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm trying to cast my mind back to this testimony and what I watched. But I think we have a confusion here about the fourth floor. This is actually the third floor, because where I come from the ground floor is not counted. That's the explanation, I think. That's, I think, where the problem lies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So it's not the position of the Defence that the school of theology was a three-storey building but it was a four-storey building, "four storeys" meaning ground floor, three upper floors?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, and I think we are talking about the third floor all the time. We are not talking about the fourth floor, counting the ground floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's -- I'm trying to avoid the whole matter by saying a four-storey building, which means four layers above the ground. And when you are talking about the top floor, whether you call it the --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I'm referring to is a building with a ground floor and three upper floors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which means four storeys in total.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it would assist the Defence, there is, of course, some other evidence as well that there were four floors. For example, DP6 told the Court that the tallest building was the monastery, that is, the faculty of theology, four floors. There is, however, other evidence which says that the tallest part had three floors. So if the Defence says that it's their position that it's not four floors but three, then the Prosecution's request makes sense in respect of the floors. If the Defence position is that there were four floors, I would like to invite the Prosecution to tell us what still is the matter at stake. Yes, please, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, in my mind it was perhaps both of each because I remember a witness who was saying that part of the building was higher than the rest and the other part of the building was lower than the one he was talking about. So it was not a question of three or four floors. And if we are talking about a building as a whole, we cannot accept that it had three or four floors because in all probability --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, if you look at the material that the Prosecution is offering, there's no way that they want to establish that the whole of the building was four floors. So you're responding to something that is, as far as I understand, not the issue raised by the Prosecution. I think the issue raised by the Prosecution is that the south-facing wing of that building had four storeys. Is that correct, Mr. Ierace?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would you please respond to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Four floors -- when we say "four floors," we mean four levels. Is this clear?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Four levels, four storeys, one ground floor, three upper floors; is that the position of the Defence, or is there -- is the position of the Defence one ground floor and two upper storeys?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Acceptable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So four storeys -- well, acceptable, yes. It's then accepted by the Defence. Mr. Ierace, may I then ask you what's the -- whether there's any use to maintain the photographs which demonstrate the height of the building and the testimony that should establish that both during and after the war the highest part of the building was four storeys?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, as I now understand it the Defence position is that the buildings -- that the highest building in the complex was indeed ground plus three upper storeys. And if that is the case, then there is no longer a conflict in the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And therefore, I don't seek to call that witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So the -- on the basis of the position of the Defence, the request to call -- to present the statement of Mr. Babic has been withdrawn. Yes. And the same is true, I would take it then, for the photographs related to his statements?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please respond -- there was a specific issue where it seemed that there was no contradiction between the parties any more. Could you please briefly respond to the other, both 92 bis issues and the viva voce witness. I think the first one addressed by the Defence for Berkovac and Bijedic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Ierace. Before leaving the issue of the photographs, I have one photograph here and I would like to be sure which part of the building is depicted. It's the one 600, the one that shows the four-storey building. Which part is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm just trying to identify which photograph 600 is. The photographs I have contain ERNs -- excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: It says "building 1."

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: I would like to know which part is the north, south, east, west, or south-east or south-west. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes. Unfortunately, Your Honour, the contents of the statement don't make that clear. There's no comment in the statement as to the position of the buildings, in terms of north, south, east, and west, I don't think. The buildings are identified by the -- otherwise by the reference at the top of each -- above each photograph, in this case "building 1" corresponds to paragraph 19, so it would seem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: So you don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then could you please, apart from the Babic statement and the photographs of the school of theology, could you please briefly respond to the other suggested rebuttal evidence in view of the response of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Just give me one moment, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, in relation to the Defence arguments which are advanced in respect of those two witnesses, the Defence, I note, at one point indicates that it would be appropriate to question the witnesses if they were called in a way that suggests beyond the strict issue in respect of which they would be called. It's my submission that that involves a misunderstanding of the purpose of rebuttal evidence. The Prosecution is limited quite strictly in calling witnesses in rebuttal. They -- I notice my learned colleague is on her feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I would just like to be able to follow which two witnesses are concerned. I am not sure which witnesses are in question. Perhaps I wasn't following carefully enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I suggested --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is it Mr. Berkovac and Mr. Bijedic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I suggested to the Prosecution to follow the order you have in your response, and that's Berkovac and Bijedic. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: So Mr. President, that's the first observation I make the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you one question directly in respect of that. So you do interpret Rule 90(H) to in this respect, that if we are talking about rebuttal evidence, that cross-examination is limited to anything that's of importance to the Defence own case only to the extent that it would be admissible in rebuttal. That means that they are not entirely free to elicit from a rebuttal testimony -- or from a rebuttal witness all information for their case but it should be limited to material that would be admissible as rebuttal evidence for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Precisely, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: It should be confined strictly to that -- that one issue or at least those issues which arise properly as rebuttal -- as rebuttal issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's clear. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: In relation to paragraph 21, the Defence argues that the issues involved are so closely connected to the role of the accused as to offend the constraints of Rule 92 bis. Mr. President, I would dispute that. The issue is in effect the positions of weaponry and other military installations, and therefore the positions of what, in one sense, might be legitimate military targets. In my respectful submission Rule 92 bis is not affected by that, in terms of its application to this particular set of facts. Moving on, Mr. President, at paragraph 22 the Defence more particularly focuses on the proposed evidence of Witness Berkovac, and I note in passing there appears to be a reference to an intent, if he was called, to go beyond the issue. But I think we've dealt with that. Mr. President, I should say that the relevance of the evidence also extends to having regard to the content of the statements, whether there were signs that the military facilities were indeed targeted in any event; in other words, whether it's consistent with the hypothetical theory that these were the targets and not Kosevo Hospital. Mr. President, unless you want to hear further from me in relation to those two witnesses --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Perhaps if you -- perhaps it's very practical if we immediately put questions to you in respect of this. As far as my recollection goes, it has always been the Defence case that if civilians were hit, that it was always a -- well, to say stray bullets or collateral damage of targeting military targets at least. That has been one of the central issues I noticed in the Defence case and it has been put to, I would say, almost all, if not all, the Prosecution witnesses. Is there any reason why the Defence -- why the Prosecution has not presented any evidence as to the military targets they considered to be in existence and therefore excluding in that view the possibility of targeting military targets rather than civilians? I mean, it has been the central issue. Of course, one of the ways to establish that you're targeting civilians is to precisely point out that it was civilians that were hit. But on the other side, you could also establish that there were no or only a very limited number of military targets around, so that that could not explain civilians to be hit. What's the reason why the Prosecution comes up with this issue in rebuttal rather than already in its -- in the presentation of its case?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, I think really there are two questions that you've posed to me. The first is to partly use your words why has the Prosecution not presented any evidence as to the military targets they considered to be in existence? In response to that question, the Prosecution called General Karavelic, who gave evidence in cross-examination as well as evidence in chief of the positioning of various military facilities in Sarajevo. There was similar evidence given by General Hadzic. So Mr. President, with respect, I don't think it's entirely correct to say that there has been no evidence called in the Prosecution case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Perhaps I should -- I should be more precise to say why no evidence has been presented specifically on these issues. I do agree with you that it can't be said that the Prosecution did not present any evidence as to military facilities, which could be military targets, but not specifically as far as I -- as my recollection goes in relation to -- to incidents to say as far as this incident is concerned there were no military targets just around. I mean, it's rather in the positive way to say here were military facilities and therefore they could be considered as military targets but not specifically on the absence of military targets around places where -- where the Prosecution claims Defence -- civilians were hit, either by shelling or by sniping.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes. In relation to the sniping incidents, Mr. President, the incidents -- the evidence surrounding the particular incidents preclude that as a plausible explanation. In other words, the evidence will typically be that there was one shot, that there was not the indicia of outgoing fire from that area at the time, there were not -- there was no military activity occurring in the vicinity as to where the person was shot, there were not people carrying weapons in that area at the time, there were not military vehicles in that area at the time, the weather was clear so as to preclude any difficulty of visibility, that sort of thing. So Mr. President, the Prosecution takes the view that it's not essential to lead evidence of what military facilities may have been nearby. If I could perhaps illustrate that with a hypothetical example: If one -- perhaps as an example, number one, the unscheduled first incident -- takes that as an example, what difference would it make if it happened that there was a brigade headquarters immediately behind the victim in terms of a line of sight. Her evidence was that there was no one on the streets at the time, there was no one nearby, that the person who attended her when she was wounded came from a nearby building. Her evidence was also that there was no sound of any firing whatsoever, that eerily quiet because of the earlier broadcast radio message. So if there would have been even a brigade headquarters a matter of metres away, it would in no way have excused her shooting, a woman wearing a dress, not carrying weapons, passing down the street. In other words, the hypothetical existence in this example of brigade headquarters is against the background of dual-use streets, if you like, a dual-use area, military and civilian. The Defence, and indeed a commander in that situation, is not excused if civilians are hit deliberately or recklessly. So Mr. President, that's the short answer to it. In relation to the scheduled shelling incidents, there has also been explanation of what military facilities were nearby. You may recall for instance, as an example of course, in relation to the Markale a number of witnesses were asked by the Prosecution in chief in the Prosecution case whether they were aware of any facilities in that area. And the same applies to the other scheduled shelling incidents. In relation to unscheduled shelling incidents there has been some evidence of some military facilities in the vicinity in relation to the Alipasino Polje incidents of the -- I think it was the 9th and 10th of November is, 1993. I do not suggest that that evidence in any way absolves those responsible of responsibility; in other words, those who carried out the actions of criminal responsibility. I simply point to in that particular instance some evidence of military facilities nearby. So Mr. President, I hope that answers your -- your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, to some extent. Because what you explained to us is that you -- that the Prosecution, as far as the presence or the absence of military facilities were concerned or military targets, military activity, has led evidence mainly by those who were at these places and observed no military activity or no military facilities. And now I would say it's a more technical presentation that you are seeking now.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I mean, if you say that we sufficiently established that, aren't you reinforcing your case by having these military professionals to support what these mainly civilian people observed?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I understand your question, Mr. President. You may recall that there was a pattern repeated almost without exception in the cross-examination of Prosecution witnesses by the Defence whereby a list of names would be rattled off to the witness and they would be invited to respond if the names meant anything to them. In that fashion - and I'm not being critical - the Defence elicited from each witness what knowledge they might have of the existence of various brigades, battalions, headquarters, paramilitary units, and so on. In that fashion, they sought to, as I understood it, obtain what evidence they could from Prosecution witnesses of the places of various legitimate military targets, otherwise legitimate, in the city. When, however, it came to their case, they called witnesses - and I think the second witness from recollection was a prime example, someone who was familiar with the area immediately to the south of Kosevo Hospital - to indicate with great specificity, including the names of streets, the appearance of buildings, particular headquarters of local units. That had not been put to General Karavelic and at a bare minimum it should have been. So we then had, for the first time and with no warning, evidence of what appeared to be significant military facilities within close proximity of Kosevo Hospital. That is why it arose and that is how it arose for the first time without warning. Now, in response, the Prosecution, through its investigators, has made relevant inquiries, and in some respects, I should say, this further evidence on one level is of assistance to the Defence, having been given this information and making relevant inquiries, the Prosecution is able to confirm that some of the -- some facilities of that nature did exist in the general area of Kosevo, not all and not to the same extent. But given this information for the first time, those inquiries are, unfortunately, made for the first time in the Defence case. Had it been put to General Karavelic, those inquiries would have been made in the Prosecution case if indeed they were needed, because of course General Karavelic could have responded on the spot in the witness box. So Mr. President, that's the background to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And I -- as I've indicated earlier, it of course doesn't then -- there remain other issues of fact, such as whether they were indeed targeted, those military facilities and whether that assists the Defence in terms of explaining any fire received at Kosevo Hospital. But I won't go into that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Whether the Defence feels assisted by your offer of rebuttal evidence from the response, I do not feel --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- That they agree with you. Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, very briefly. We would like to thank the Prosecution for attempting to assist us in this manner, but we do not share their point of view for the simple reason that when we examined --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... It's clear that you do not share their view. So if there's any --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope that it's clear, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But as far as Karavelic is concerned, what we want to say in clear terms - because we are being reproached with not having questioned Karavelic in detail, in sufficient detail - when we are asking -- when this witness was asked a series of questions, he was subject to amnesia, he no longer knew whether there were any tanks or whether there were any heavy weapons, he didn't know anything any more. So why question a witness who is not prepared to answer? That's my first point. And the second point is that the Defence is examining and will inform very soon this Trial Chamber the possibility of submitting a motion so that this witness is accused of perjury because we think that a chief, a corps commander, cannot be unaware of the number of heavy weapons he has in such a situation. The responses he provided are being examined in detail, and perhaps we will intervene again to ask for article -- for Rule 91 to be applied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do not -- I must be quite honest. I do not understand your last remark. Rule 91 being to ask witnesses not to -- to tell witnesses not to lie? Is that -- let me just have a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do not -- at this moment I do not see that as any request for Mr. Karavelic to be -- to be examined.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I said that -- no, Mr. President, I said that the Defence counsel is in the course of examining the possibility of following procedure before your Trial Chamber so that this witness who obviously did not say the truth, something should be -- some measures should be taken against him. And I am quoting Rule 91, which has to do with false testimony before the Trial Chamber. That's another matter that I just wanted to inform you of this in advance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. An observation that that's another matter. Then the next question would be the witnesses Vladimir Sisic, and Vahida Makic. That is, I would say, the mosques. Mr. Ierace, would you please response to the response of the Prosecution -- of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I find the argument of the Defence in relation to these two witnesses perhaps a little self-contradictory. But in any event, the evidence became relevant -- I withdraw that. As I've indicated in my written explanation, there was peripheral reference to this issue in the Prosecution case, quite peripheral. And in the Defence case it became a matter of constant questioning of Prosecution -- of Defence witnesses as to whether they were aware of mosques being damaged. Looking at the arguments of the Defence, the -- at paragraph 31 the Defence submitted that the statements mention facts which go to proof of acts and conduct of the accused. Well, strictly speaking, the issue was whether mosques had been damaged. That was the way in which it initially arose in the Defence case. But the Defence went on to elicit evidence from witnesses that mosques had not been targeted by forces of the accused. The basis of relevance offered by the Defence was whether -- was a matter of consistency, given the accused wasn't charged with those matters, the Defence argument was one would expect mosques to be at least damaged and one might infer if indeed not targeted if there was a campaign in existence to target civilians. Now, Mr. President, the evidence in rebuttal makes clear that in those two examples mosques were damaged and indeed, in one instance, were targeted. If the Trial Chamber takes the view, if you take the view, Mr. President and Your Honours, that there is too close a nexus between these acts and the accused, thus requiring him to be called, then we could do that, we could call each of those two witnesses. In relation to the mosque in the area of Dobrinja and Nedzarici, I think there were a series of witnesses. I think in my explanation I referred to two, there were others as well, who were specifically asked about that mosque, whether that mosque was damaged. And so it takes on particular significance. Thank you. Do you wish me to go on to the next witness, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm just trying to verify whether I understood the parties well. You, Mr. Ierace, said the Prosecution did not consider the damage or even destruction of mosques of great relevance. It was just a peripheral matter for you. And you're now offering this evidence in rebuttal because the Defence, by repeatedly asking questions about damage done to mosques, has given it a different type of relevance and that relevance would be that if you -- if you attack Muslim civilians, not just by mistake but as a system, systematic way, then you would not -- you would also attack mosques. It's not well understandable that you do attack the Muslims systematically and do not attack their mosques. Is that a correct understanding of the Defence position and also a correct understanding of the reason why you want to present this evidence in rebuttal?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Indeed -- Mr. President, they're not my words. They're the words of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, Mr. Ierace, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: They're not my words. They're the -- they're a paraphrasing of the words of the Defense when the issue was first deliberated upon by the Trial Chamber. And I think I give the page reference in the -- in my written explanation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. There is a matter which is in dispute, a matter of contention between us. But what we want to emphasise is that it's not quite true to say that this wasn't included in the indictment with regard to the charges levelled against General Galic. I think that in the indictment it mentions a campaign that was either inherited or implemented by General Galic and the objective of this campaign was to hit very symbolic buildings such as museums, historical buildings, et cetera. And it is obvious that if one is opposed to a people called the Muslims, then it is obvious that the monuments that express the identity and culture of this people, so religious buildings, it is obvious that they will necessarily be included in the indictment. If the Prosecution didn't think of clarifying this point in the course of its case, well, that's not the Defence's problem. The Defence says this and it has proved the fact that the mosques in Sarajevo with a few exceptions due to firing errors, we claim that mosques were not targeted, and this is an element of proof indicating that there was no campaign. That is our position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's clear. Thank you. Then let's move to the next -- well, the next one in the response of the Defence is the Babic statement, which seems not --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I think we've dealt with that one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we've dealt with that one. Then we have --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Linda Patrick in the process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, in relation to Professor Zecevic, Mr. Stamp will deal with that. But before I hand over to him -- might I just note for the record that as I understand it, this is the first time the Defence has suggested that mosques in Sarajevo were indeed hit, and I quote the words appearing at page 23, line 9, "due to firing errors." Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Mr. President, Mr. Ierace is very artful. He said that although this wasn't targeted, there were traces. Obviously there were. Sarajevo was a city at war and it's quite probable that there were certain holes, certain bursts on the walls. The Defence counsel can't know what the state of all the mosques were. We can't say that bullets never hit a certain wall, the wall of a mosque, et cetera. That's obvious. We shouldn't be -- words shouldn't be put in the mouth of the Defence, and certainly not in this manner. It's not very agreeable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You have explained your position on this issue. Then, Mr. Ierace, we come to -- we'll not deal with Dr. Zecevic at this time but Jonathan Tait-Harris, and Ademir Hadzismailovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. President. In relation to Jonathan Tait-Harris, the first part -- I withdraw that. I notice Mr. Piletta-Zanin is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry to interrupt, but again the transcript is very liberal, as far as the English booth is concerned. I said a moment ago it was very important that I say it again. It's possible that hits were made not only against mosques but also against churches. It doesn't appear in the transcript, and it's important. A bullet could have hit a mosque, a synagogue, or a church, and I think this has to be made very clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's clear. One of the reasons, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, why it might be difficult to have everything in the transcript is also the speed of speech. And I know that we are all violating now and then. But a slower speed of speech certainly will make the task -- the very difficult task of those who have to transcribe the hearing and to translate whatever has been said at least a little bit less difficult, as it is not easy. Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the first part of Jonathan Tait-Harris's proposed evidence is dealt with at paragraph 50 of the Defence response, and the response of the Defence is to claim that they have "proved," and I quote that word, indeed I'll quote the rest of the sentence "proved that these are authentic SRK documents through its witnesses," and then mentions some witnesses, including Dr. Radinovic. And concludes, "The statement of this witness is not relevant for a decision of the Trial Chamber in present case." Mr. President, this material becomes relevant for the first time in rebuttal because one was entitled to expect that the Defence would establish the authenticity of these documents that it sought to tender in its own case. Indeed, it could not do it during the Prosecution case. It had to be done during the Defence case. But did we hear a witness say "I found these documents in this place," "this is how they were stored since 1994 or 1995"? No, we did not. The Prosecution has consistently maintained its position throughout that accepting the broad parameters which apply in this Tribunal the documents would be admitted subject to the issue of weight and that we did not accept that they had been authenticated but we would take whatever steps we could to satisfy ourselves that they were authentic. So it's relevant to that issue of weight. It could not be done in the Prosecution case. It could only be done in rebuttal. And it rebuts in effect, to put it in a strict context, evidence in the Defence case which tends to suggest the documents are authentic. Coming to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you one question in that respect: If it is your position that the source of at least many of these documents is rather vague or unclear, would -- first of all, the question is whether it would be the Prosecution's task to establish that it's unclear where -- or is it in your view the task of the Defence to establish that the source of these documents is clear? And that leads me to the second question, that is: Do you consider the evidence you suggest to present of assistance to make clear to the Chamber that the sources are unclear, or would that be clear enough without such evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. President, in response to the first question, it is incumbent upon the Defence and the Defence alone to sufficiently establish the authenticity, if you like the antecedents of the documents. The reason that we lead this evidence of what the Prosecution has done in that regard is, in one sense, an exercise in completing the story, because if this was not done, then the Trial Chamber might reasonably or perhaps -- at least, I could take out "reasonably," -- might conclude on the state of its present knowledge that there was the imparting of relevant information at the meeting that took place between investigators, and of course that was made aware to the Trial Chamber. So the onus rests squarely with the Defence. This makes clear that nothing further was open to the Prosecution and that doesn't shift the onus. In relation to the second question - might I just refresh my memory on that one-

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think your answer covered more or less both questions or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, I think it does, Mr. President. And indeed, Mr. Radinovic in his report commented that the documents had been dispersed. Mr. President, just in relation to that, I don't know if it's of assistance to the Trial Chamber at this stage - I think we have said it in the past - that in particular where the documents assist the Defence, unless they're authenticated, they should not attract any significant weight. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, in your response in this -- on this part, am I right that the issue of to what extent authentication has been offered, has been dealt with as complete as possible? Because I do read that you say, well, for -- that some witnesses have identified certain documents. I take it that you're specifically referring to -- to witnesses who say I recognise this document, I drafted it myself or I signed it or whatever, but I know it, and it's -- I think you also referred in your response to -- well, what seems to suggest an authentication by your military expert. Is that correct and could you explain more specifically what you understand by authentication by your military expert, since it is my recollection that very often documents are used or produced without a clear origin of it mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. The problem of the collection of documents was covered by several witnesses. The knot was untied. Some documents were scattered all over the place, and I cannot make a judgment on this but I can establish even now that what the Defence actually did when making efforts to adduce this evidence is rather important. Now, when we considered useful to ask everyone who had any knowledge about these facts their opinion of the authenticity of these documents. So the witness sometimes said "I know the person who signed it," or "this is the format in which documents were usually drafted and I can confirm it's authentic." On the other hand, the military expert had said that he had had opportunity to review all these documents. He had access to dozens of binders containing such documents. Secondly, based on his career and his military competences, he was in a position to know whether a certain order was an order which was formally acceptable or adequate in legal and formal terms. He was able to compare orders between them, and he could ascertain whether a certain order was the usual format that was issued within a certain corps or brigade. Secondly, after this internal comparison, the military expert gave a very precise opinion on these documents. This question will come up again, and we will deal with it again when we talk about the military experts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 8, 28 line 8 it said that the --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, I don't have the same numbering because I again stopped my computer and in fact I said really that the corps was disbanded. Thank you, Honourable Judge. The corps simply disappeared as some sort of military organisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's a clear position from the Defence. Mr. Ierace, then we have Mr. From.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I think, Mr. President, before we get to that there's the part of Jonathan Tait-Harris's statement that relates to Witness G.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And the argument of the Defence is that, as I understand it, that if the -- firstly, that the medical certificate is not an appropriate way to introduce the -- in effect the evidence of the doctor. But as I've indicated in the written explanation, the doctor is available for us to call him as a witness. Mr. President, the Defence argument in relation to this issue generally as a rebuttal issue - and that, of course, includes the photographs of back of Witness G - overlook the fact that the witness offered to bare his back in the court and show the precise positions of the wounds. They did not ask him to do that on cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. -- Yes, Mr. Ierace. It's my recollection that when he offered to do so that you said it's not necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: No, that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: No, I'm not seeking to be clever here, Mr. President. That was in chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it was in chief, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And listening to that, the Defence would have well understood that when it came their turn later in the evidence if they had wanted to see those wounds, they could have asked him to go that extra step and reveal where the wounds were on his back. That's my point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And when I said those words to him "no, it's not necessary" that is because I reasonably understood it was not an issue. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. We don't have to spend too much time on that, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At this point I'm falling off my chair because in this case we're only talking about knowing what's left and what's right. Carefully looking at the file and God knows how many people are in the Prosecution team to do this, would have permitted us to establish facts. So we cannot say to someone, "Look, here is the right and here is the left." This is something that the Prosecution team should have done. They had enough elements to do that, and they could have shown the witness's back if they wanted to. And now it's a bit too late to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You say the Prosecution could have pointed at the contradiction between -- yes, the Defence could have done the same. That's -- we have a report and we have a witness who stated where it was. We are now in a position where we have to decide whether any rebuttal evidence will be heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I haven't yesterday responded to that part of the Defence argument in -- that is the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The left-right business. Lead counsel for the Defence speaks as her native tongue and reads B/C/S. If the Defence was of the view that the relevant part of the medical report clearly indicated a left-right trajectory which was inconsistent with their case, that should have been put to the witness, and it wasn't, in spite of repeated warnings in relation to that rule. It, therefore, emerged for the first time in the Defence case, and the Prosecution has responded appropriately. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President, I do not agree because the Prosecution focuses -- the Defence focuses its efforts toward what is appropriate and it's not up to the Defence to do this job, and the Defence does not have the material resources to examine all the details. It was only much later that the Defence was able, with the assistance of its experts, to examine certain points and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We don't have to fully debate this issue, whether -- I noticed that, at least during the presentation of the evidence and the cross-examination the matter was not identified -- the issue was not identified at this moment. Then any more about Mr. Tait-Harris, apart from Witness G?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one thing that I would like to add with regard to Mr. Radovic [as interpreted], with your leave. It's -- the witness mentioned a minute ago. No, it's not necessary. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ierace, any further issues in relation to --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, there was a further issue covered in the statement of Mr. Tait-Harris, but I don't know that the Defence has responded to it, and that was the nature of the terrain between the school of theology and the area approximate to, I think it was incident 23.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it was the --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And I must say in relation to that issue, Mr. President, whilst indeed there was a witness who said it was open terrain, thereby I think suggesting that there was no opportunity for a sniper to operate closer to the front line. In fairness I should point out that there were some other Defence witnesses who is said there was indeed cover there. They didn't use that word but they referred to houses and to trees. And so I -- I couldn't suggest that the unequivocal Defence evidence was that there was no cover. And if you did not -- if you were against the Prosecution in terms of that as being rebuttal evidence, the Prosecution at least has other Defence evidence it could point to in relation to that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is not a real withdrawal of this aspect, or is it? Or is it just a relativation of the importance of this issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: There's a conflict in the Defence evidence, and that makes it a little difficult, I think, to -- for the Prosecution to determine whether we are obliged to refute it, that is, refute the evidence of one of their witnesses when other witnesses take a different view. Ideally we would call that evidence, but given the constraints which are upon all of us, should the Trial Chamber decide that we cannot call that evidence, then I would say nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is there any response specifically in this respect, Ms. Pilipovic or Mr. Piletta-Zanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the stance of the Defence being that there had never been snipers outside this building. Everything else follows as a castle of cards. The thing with this witness is again another difficulty for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then Mr. Ierace, the next issue is --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. From.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the nature of his evidence, his anticipated evidence, could be neatly divided into two aspects, the first being the so-called line of sight rebuttal evidence. In relation to that, the Defence argument appears to be, looking at paragraph 57, that it's not possible to establish lines of sight from these maps because they do not contain the data of building heights, tree densities, and so on. Now, Mr. President, I don't think we've disclosed a copy of the -- these maps other than for incident 24, which was one of the Jewish cemetery incidents. And I think the Prosecution disclosed to you at that stage, as we disclosed to the Defence, a graph and a map, and that is the type of evidence that we're talking about in relation to these five other incidents. So my first point is, in response to the Defence argument, that the essential aspect of this evidence is, if you like, the graph showing the fall of the land between the suspected source of fire and the position of the victim. And in relation to incidents 4, 9, and 14, in particular in relation to incident 4, Witness G at least, one will note that the land falls away very steeply from the source of fire. So one certainly in that case doesn't need to know the heights of buildings, because there weren't any. There's no evidence there were any in between. The suggestion by the Defence was there were orchards and forests at the time, and the fall of the land is of assistance to the Trial Chamber in determining whether that, assuming that there were such things, that that would have indeed been an obstruction to the line of sight. In relation to incident 24, there is indeed some evidence as to the height of the chapel in the cemetery, and that was the relevant aspect there. You may recall I put to the witness there was a 40-metre difference between the chapel at ground level and his position, and the map made clear there was a direct line of sight between his position through the chapel to the site of the -- where the victim was hit and therefore whether the chapel was beneath the line of sight was relevant. So Mr. President, my basic position is the Defence argument doesn't really respond to the relevant aspect of the Prosecution evidence for category 1. Category 2 is not evidence in rebuttal. And that's the -- the maps which are now possible with software which has been available to us since November 2002, and that software allows the measurement of distances more conveniently on the maps with a ruler because they contain a scale.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you one question in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say it's available to us since November 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That can mean two different things. The first is that it's on the market since November 2002; it also can mean that you bought it in November 2002 but it was on the market already for ten months. Could you explain more clearly what it means "available to you," on the market or in your office?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, in our office. The mapping people purchased that software, it became available to them in November 2002. I don't know when it first came on to the market. And it was with the arrival of that software that it was possible to do these additional features, such as graphs, and I first made the Trial Chamber aware of it in the second half of November, I think towards the end of November; in other words, within a few weeks of it coming into the office. Thank you, Mr. President. I should add, if you need to be aware of it, that there have been some difficulties in providing these maps earlier than we have to the Defence. We provided the Defence with a complete set on Wednesday, another set earlier in the week, and those difficulties are of -- they're to do with a combination of factors, Mr. President. But suffice to say at this stage that that's the earliest that we could do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I think we've -- we've not forgotten but --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And Mr. President, I'm sorry to interrupt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Because it's not rebuttal evidence, I appreciate that calling this second category of evidence at this late stage is problematic because it would be in effect evidence in chief from the Prosecution. It seems to me, Mr. President, in my respectful submission that unless the Trial Chamber took the view that it was material which the Trial Chamber wished to have directly, then I would withdraw it. The Trial Chamber is empowered to have material tendered into evidence directly, and that, of course, would follow an examination of Mr. From and I should say a demonstration, complete with computer access on our monitors. But if that's not the case, then the Prosecution acknowledges that there are clear difficulties in tendering it, that is, the second category of evidence, at this late stage. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just for -- it's quarter to 4.00. I'd like, with the assistance of the interpreters and the technicians to see whether we can -- because Dr. Zecevic is still to be discussed -- to see whether we can get a brief answer by Mr. Piletta-Zanin, apart from what has already been said in the response from the Defence, and then briefly discuss Dr. Zecevic and then have the break. If that could be then, then we'd -- the break might be a bit longer than -- but if there's a problem ...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: No problem for the interpreters, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There's -- as far as the technicians are concerned, there's ten minutes of tape left, so we certainly could not surpass that ten minutes. If the interpreters would be willing to cooperate, then we'll have an adequate break afterwards. Please, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. And the Defence counsel would like to thank all the booths too. Mr. President, if my memory is correct, the Prosecution case started in October -- sometime in October 2002. We have had a lot of difficulties -- the Defence for General Galic has had a lot of difficulties when we had to deal with these maps which weren't regular in that they were artificially stretched, extended. The Defence counsel say that is it was handicapped because of this, and we see that the maps that we are shown now are maps where the scale is quite correct and you no longer have this distortion, and it would have been extremely useful for General Galic's Defence if we had been in a position to have these maps during the proceedings. The Prosecution has never told us. We now have a solution. "Let's discuss it. Let's have a look at it, let's examine it," and this is something which is a serious problem with regard to respecting the rights of the parties. And we think that it is now far too late to use these maps. This is technically no longer possible. But it is our opinion that the Prosecution should have provided these maps earlier; that was its obligation and it didn't do so for reasons which seem to us to be evident. They didn't want to carry out one of its obligations in this field. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, could I respond very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes. When this issue was considered in November, Mr. President, you will recall that you asked me if it was possible for some maps to be made at the instructions of the Defence, and I assured you we would find ways to do that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then Dr. Zecevic. That's, I think, the last issue we have as far as the rebuttal evidence is concerned. Could I please hear the response from the Prosecution to the position taken by the Defence. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. And I have to admit that I don't master it to a certain extent. I know that the Trial Chamber does. In principle, if this expert witness should be heard again, it's obvious that Dr. Vilicic should also be heard again. This would be fair, for the sake of equality of arms. utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Though the issue of a sort of balance, that is, if one is to be heard, then the other is to be heard again, may be something that the Court might think it appropriate to consider later at an appropriate time, the issues which Dr. Zecevic proposes to -- or we propose that Dr. Zecevic deals with in rebuttal are issues which were fully and completely canvassed by the Defence when they had Dr. Vilicic in chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I take it that if you say, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, if the expert witness should be heard again, it's obvious that Dr. Vilicic should also be heard again. I take it that if Dr. Zecevic would testify and if after hearing his testimony the Defence would consider it important to hear Dr. Vilicic again, that you'll ask leave to call him in rejoinder evidence and the Chamber then, of course, if this happens, will consider whether this evidence qualifies to be heard in rejoinder. Then I would like to adjourn for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll adjourn until 4.30. We'll then deal with the other matters, that is, mainly the exhibits. And if the Chamber is able to give decisions, even if they were just oral decisions for the time being, we'll let the parties know. There is another issue I'd like to parties to think about, that is, next Thursday the Chamber is requested to swap with another case. So that would mean that we would sit next Thursday, if we are sitting at all, but then to sit in the afternoon and not in the morning. I'd like to hear from the parties whether there's any objection against that. And if there would be an objection against Thursday, would then the parties please consider whether that would be possible, but that's only a second choice, on Wednesday next week. We'll adjourn until 4.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber apologises for returning late, but we thought it of great importance to give decisions right away and then take ten more minutes for that. The Prosecution has requested leave to present rebuttal evidence. First of all, a statement that was provided to the Chamber in relation to interception of telephone conversations of a certain Mr. Suman was not explained by the Prosecution, and the Chamber understood it to be a mistake that this evidence was also sought to be presented. Is that correct, Mr. Ierace?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Not a mistake, Mr. President, but I don't have anything to submit to you on that, the -- other than to say the obvious. You may recall that in the last few days of the Defence case a transcript was shown to a witness, to Mr. Radinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And I think something was said on that occasion. I don't seek to say anything further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, no further explanation has been given, since the Defence has had hardly any opportunity to respond to what would have been the reasons for the appearance of Mr. Suman as a viva voce witness. In this respect, the request is denied. But before continuing, the Chamber would like to set out very briefly what in its view qualifies as rebuttal evidence, that is, evidence in relation to a significant issue is the first criterium; the second criterium, that it arises directly out of Defence evidence; and the third criterium, that it could not be reasonably anticipated by the party who seeks that rebuttal evidence to present that rebuttal evidence. I'll on the basis of this go through the -- through the request in respect of other witnesses, either -- and we'll start with the other viva voce witness, Mr. From. In respect of the first part of the evidence to be given by Mr. From, the Chamber does not consider it to be proper rebuttal evidence. And as far as the second part is concerned, it would be fresh evidence, and therefore the request is denied. Then we have, and I'll deal with them together, the 92 bis statements of Makic and Sisic, that's -- to say it short, that's about the -- about the mosques. This trying of -- or targeting mosques is not a part of the Prosecution's case, at least not an explicit part of the Prosecution's case, and the issue is not of such significance as to qualify as rebuttal evidence. I then come to Dr. Zecevic. That needs perhaps a bit more explanation. Dr. Zecevic has testified during the Prosecution's case about the speed a projectile would need to have its tail fin embedded into the ground. So penetration in the ground and speed of impact were matters explicitly dealt with during the Prosecution's case. During the Defence case, Dr. Vilicic has further elaborated on that, especially he has given tables and Berezansky formula. After having heard all this evidence and having seen what the Prosecution offers as new evidence, in the opinion of the Chamber there is not a remaining issue of sufficient significance to deal with in rebuttal. Therefore, also in this respect, the request is denied. The evidence to be given by Mr. Tait-Harris. Mr. Tait-Harris deals with a couple of matters. The only one on which the Chamber would allow Mr. Tait-Harris -- the statement of Mr. Tait-Harris to be presented in evidence would be the photograph of the back of Witness G, not the medical report of the doctor attached to it but just the photograph. And the Defence will have 15 minutes for cross-examination of Mr. Tait-Harris on this photograph. Then evidence to be given by Mr. Babic, that request is withdrawn. Is same is true for Linda Patrick. That's of no importance any more. And then finally the evidence to be presented by Mr. Berkovac and Mr. Bijedic, that could sufficiently be anticipated by the Prosecution and therefore in that respect the request is also denied. That means the only witness who has to be called and whose statement and only to a very limited extent can be presented in rebuttal evidence is Mr. Tait-Harris, exclusively on Witness G. These are the decisions -- it's the decision of the Chamber on the request of the Prosecution. Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I just want to clarify something. I wasn't quite listening to the English booth. The French booth mentioned 50 minutes. That's quite generous. But should I take it to be 15 minutes, as it states in the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll accept that gladly, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Having regard to the decision in respect to Dr. Zecevic, I just note that the decision referred to one part of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

The Chamber Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then having given these decisions, we should move to the outstanding exhibits of different character.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. We wanted to ask your Trial Chamber to proceed a little more slowly, perhaps, because we have to check all of this. But what we wanted to say is that we received from the Prosecution about 16 pages -- no --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm talking about the witness Radovanovic, the demographer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, the Chamber is a bit confused, as a matter of fact, to whether there were -- what the problem -- what kind of problems there were in respect of these bundles. These were the bundles, the lists of --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The bundles, the two bundles, are -- let us deal with the last two bundles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What were we to consider as matters which the Court could legitimately consider. utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And noted that they bore official stamps. So there were two things, the weight and the -- which is an ultimate issue, but also what is really admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I regret not having been here for the end of the hearing of this witness because I could have personally clarified some of these points. I'll do so now. These documents were provided, and we know that they all come from the Prosecution. So as far as the authenticity is concerned, as Judge Nieto-Navia said, there shouldn't be any problems. These documents were provided so that the witness could tell us what his impression as a professional was about what one could have done on the basis of such a document, in purely statistical terms. And I think that there is no reason to reject them because the witness recognised them as documents that he was accustomed to see, and given the fact that he could find his bearings there, he could identify them, certain conclusions could be reached which were useful for his report and could have made it possible to compare his report with the other expert reports. So it doesn't seem useful for us in our opinion to reject such a document and it's not desirable either. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's the position of the Defence. We'll give a decision not right away, but it does not influence in whatever way -- Yes, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.text: Just an inquiry. I was wondering if counsel's last remarks were addressed to Radinovic or Radovanovic.

utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

That will happen, but not yet. I may have spoken about an expert in the masculine, but I was referring to a woman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That is then clarified as well. That's rather a language matter. Then we have in relation to Witness DP30. utterances.text: That's the interview of which the Chamber said that it would consider admission if it would be presented in such a way that I think I referred to that last Tuesday what exactly was required to make the Chamber consider to admit it into evidence. utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, just before that happens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.text: Perhaps I should clarify. I think on the last occasion we sought to tender some cassettes. And I now think that there were already some cassettes. No.

utterances.text: I think we wanted the cassette, the original with the translation on it, so that we could hear everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that we would have the transcripts and --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE

utterances.text: Yes. So it's now up to the Defence to express itself on whether it wants to object.

utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence has no objection to the admission of this document, but in view of the fact that this document was corrected by the witness and that the witness answered questions by investigators and the document isn't signed, you will have to decide what weight to attach to it and how to estimate its authenticity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Being no objection against admission, it is admitted into evidence. Madam Registrar, could you please call them.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P3766, under seal, interview -- just a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In view of the confidentiality, we'll first now move into private session.

utterances.text: We are in open session again. The registrar just referred to documents P2754 and P2759 that were tendered through Witness DP17. Is there any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.text: Then these two documents are admitted into evidence. Then we have in respect of Witness Milenko Indic, document P3785. Madam Registrar, that is ...?

utterances.text: Exhibit P3785 is "report of the Secretary-General pursuant to general assembly resolution 53/35, the fall of Srebrenica."

utterances.text: Yes. Although, not the whole of the report. I think it's the front page, it's the --

utterances.text: There are two pages dealing with the Markale market incident, and these are pages ...?

Mr. Mundis.
