utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution would object to that portion of D1930A that contains the English translations on the grounds that those translations were not available at the time the witness testified and thus we were unable to cross-examine the witness with respect to those pages of the book which were previously only available in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I ask you, Mr. Mundis, is my understanding correct that those parts of the book do not directly relate to any of the specific incidents but -- that's not to invalidate your objection, but do I understand that those parts of this book give explanation general and pictures in general of -- of wounds, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I believe that it's something that either came spontaneously from the witness or was a question asked by the Chamber, but I can't really remember now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It spontaneously came up. On the other hand, Mr. Mundis, the objection at that time was that you could not -- you would object because there were no English translations. Now the English translations are there, and it's not because of the content of the articles but, rather, on the fact that there were no translations at that time that you now -- I mean, you could have foreseen that or -- or was your objection at that time already that it could never be admitted because there were no English translations at that very moment when the witness was in court?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No, it would be the former, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then it's a bit surprising that -- if you say it cannot be admitted because there are no English translations and not purely because at the moment of the testimony there were no English translations that you ask English translations to be made and then to say, "well, they were not there at that time, so even with these translations we would still object".

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Perhaps -- perhaps I wasn't clear, Mr. President. When this issue was raised on Tuesday of this week --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And I indicated that our objection had been that the materials that were provided by the registry did not include an English translation, that was referring back to when the witness testified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The fact that he pulled this out. We were then unable to cross-examine him because of that spontaneous production of this material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And that's simply the grounds for our objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand. That must then -- at least, I misunderstood what you then said on Tuesday. We'll then give a decision at a later stage on that. Then we have, Madam Registrar, the documents that are suggested to be given number C10 and C11.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Two words, because I didn't state my view on this issue. The Prosecution never mentioned this witness who could have been recalled if they needed clarification on this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand that you would take the position that by other means the matter could have been solved rather than by -- by objecting against the admission into evidence of this part of the bundle. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If I could just respond, Mr. President. The first time that I was shown the bundle of documents which the Defence proposed to tender through this witness was on Tuesday of this week. utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, it seems to be that a lot of misunderstandings have been there in what one party expected from the other. The Chamber will give a decision. utterances.text: C10 is an UNMO report from December 1992; and C11, UNMO report January 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: These documents are admitted into evidence as well. Then the next issue would be three new video sequences on one tape, the number being P3783 and P3783.1, which the last number relating to the transcript of this videotape. Madam Registrar.

utterances.text: I understand that the Prosecution intends to tender a new version of the transcript numbered P3783A.

utterances.text: Mr. President, the problem with the earlier transcript is that in clip 1 and clip 2, that is, on the transcript, there is a reference to a particular person, being a three-year-old child. utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Excuse me. I would like to say that we shouldn't go to the merits before the decision is made on these tapes. I don't know if we are allowed to state our view on this now.

utterances.text: Yes. The -- I understood that the Prosecution was just explaining why they produced a new transcript which is slightly different from the former one. utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Gladly. Mr. President, as you probably know, I didn't have the opportunity to see everything because I came from being away. I don't think it is fair to ask us to accept these tapes, which have not been seen by you, first of all, and haven't been seen by the parties. And thirdly, it was not possible for General Galic, who never ever saw them, to express his opinion or to advise his counsel, which advice is very necessary, how to proceed. So procedurally speaking, this is inadmissible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, let me just try to reconstruct what happened. Witness Gray came with a number of tapes. You used part of one of these tapes, which later on was called the fifth tape, in your sequence that you tendered into evidence. Therefore, it seems reasonable to accept that the Defence was aware of the content of that fifth tape. It could have discussed it with the accused -- well, it was only because the Prosecution could not find that sequence on the four tapes disclosed to it that they felt that there should have been another tape, and it was only after quite some time where both parties tried to do our best -- their best - and I refer to my remarks regarding who came out most happy out of the weekend - both parties did their utmost best to find that tape on which this first sequence of the compilation tape tendered by the Defence could be found. It was only at the very end of this exercise that it turned out that the Defence had a tape which it had not disclosed. Now you are suggesting that the witness - and you're again, but it might be a translation error as well, but as far as I'm aware of the word "witness" has no feminine in French either, it's just "the witness" and not "the female witness." Do you want us to call Mr. Gray -- should the Defence -- should the Prosecution call Mr. Gray again? Is that what you suggest?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. What I said - I wasn't speaking of a witness in the feminine. If that was the case, I'm sorry. But I remember that Mr. Gray is not a lady - what I really said was this witness, in the masculine form, should be heard. Why? Certainly there was a mistake with the fifth tape. Certainly we offer our apologies to everyone concerned. This error was genuine, and it had to do with the haste in which we worked. But it doesn't mean that these excerpts have really not been viewed by either the Trial Chamber or the Defence or the Prosecution in the courtroom. So the most correct way and the most logical way was to call this witness to tell him, "Here are these clips, these sequences, what can you tell us about it?" Neither the Defence nor the Prosecution developed this. The best way now would be to correct this mistake. The Prosecution was then saying, "Let us remove these first two sequences in the Defence tape which are contained in some fifth tape." That's what would restore the balance between the parties in the best way. But if these three tapes are admitted - I can see that the Prosecutor is shaking his head - but if they are admitted, it is completely against the Rules of Procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I never said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I said three tapes, I meant the three sequences.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I never said that the segments on the Defence compilation tape, which we now know came from the fifth tape, should not be admitted. I have not said that, and I don't say it now. Mr. President whilst I'm on my feet, there was -- there are two further documents that I should refer to. The first is a B/C/S rough translation of the transcript of the three clips. And the final document -- perhaps I should explain in this way: During the course of the first clip, a document is seen on the screen. I don't think it's possible to read the words of that document on the copy. It is, however, perfectly clear, on the -- what I might call the original, that is, the fifth tape that was provided by the Defence. It's a document which has not many words on it. They're in B/C/S. So the third document that I seek to tender is a transcript of those words that appear on the document on the copy of the tape provided by the Defence, which perhaps we could call the original. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, the Defence also has expressed as its view that the tape should be played in open court, at least, and to be played in the presence of the accused. What's the view of the Prosecution there?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I have no objection to that, Mr. President. It would take something like nine minutes, perhaps ten minutes. The clips are a little longer than the typical clip from the other tapes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Defence also said that we -- that there should be a possibility to examine Mr. Gray on the -- on the tapes. He produced them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: By a coincidence. He was not there when finally it came into the hands of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. President, the way that was first justified, as I understand the argument, was by way of rebuttal the Prosecution should call Mr. Gray. It's not a question of rebuttal. The Prosecution accepts that it's simply not practically possible to have Mr. Gray here in order to be further cross-examined in relation to these tapes. And as I said the other day, there is no perfect solution to this problem. Because of that, I accept, the Prosecution accepts, that these tapes will now attract appropriate weight determined on the content of the tapes themselves. The Prosecution has lost the opportunity to have the witness identify events and places which appear on the tape, and we've lost the opportunity to cross-examine him in relation to a number of matters which I don't think I need to set out at this stage. So Mr. President, essentially what I'm proposing is that the tapes be tendered and appropriate weight be attributed to them in due course by the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So I take it that you're not only proposing that the tapes be tendered but even admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Admitted as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, may I first, before I give you an opportunity to respond, could I ask you the following: Events, places, what appears on that tape, could you tell us whether Mr. Gray would have any personal knowledge of these events, these places. I mean, I'm just trying to make clear for myself what it would bring if Mr. Gray would be recalled.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, may I ask you to go back into closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll turn into private session, as we usually do in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So to repeat what I said briefly, I really don't know what this witness knows or doesn't know about the possible locations that appear in certain tapes, but what I can say is that if they should be viewed, if they were to be viewed, it should be done in the presence of the witness. I want to be very clear, and I'm afraid I may have been misunderstood by someone a while ago. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is there any -- is there any rule you would like to invoke that the witness should be present if this videotape is played?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Article 20 of the Statute in that the Defence maintains that their rights would be violated if certain elements on the tape were used without the Defence being in a position to, for example, draw the attention of the Trial Chamber to certain events, certain facts. So these are the essential rights of all those who are accused. They must have access to a fair judgment. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If I understand you well, therefore you say the -- if the witness, who has now returned to another continent, could give some guidance as to what aspects of the picture shown would require specific attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Could we go back into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll return into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are now in open session again. Let me just see. I'm just trying to find out where exactly we went into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, our assistant, who is paying attention to everything, it seems, tells me that it would be page 62, line 22, but this should be checked. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. No, it was already checked by Madam Registrar, who comes to the same conclusion, so that's correct. Let me then just find out what was dealt with in private session. First there was a sequence which was intended to be in private session. Yes. Then we continued to discuss in private session that the Defence claimed that there was unclarity in respect of the chronology of the events that appear on sequences that appear on this compilation tape. We then discussed a date which appeared on a document which is shown, as far as I understand, on the videotape. It gives a date, the Prosecution told us, that therefore the events could not have taken place prior to that date but presumably on that date or after that date. But there was a relation between the first or second sequence to the extent that the first sequence had to do with a killing and the second sequence with a burial in the view of the Prosecution related to that killing, so therefore it should have been a couple of days afterwards, and that it was not certain what the date was of the third sequence. And then you, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you asked some questions about what was clear and what was not clear in this respect. I think that covers more or less what we dealt with in -- and then finally we discussed the matter on whether this tape should be played in the presence of the witness, and where Mr. Ierace suggested that we should play the tape in order to better understand what we had to decide about, that you opposed against and said that you were misunderstood and that you thought the tape could be played only in the presence of the witness. If there's anything to be added to this short summary of what was dealt with in private session, I invite the parties to do so. Otherwise, we'll proceed. Then we'll give a decision in due course on this issue. I think we then dealt with all the exhibits, apart from the Radinovic documents. And I suggest that we do that after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, there is one other document that I'm aware of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And I might have forgotten one. And that would be, Mr. Ierace?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, that would be some pages from the final report of the commission of experts. At the same time as the Trial Chamber requested a copy of the SMO January 1993 report, the Trial Chamber also requested either party to tender certain pages of the report, annex 6 of the report of the commission of experts. The Defence helpfully filed the relevant pages on the 28th of February -- 27th of February, 2003. And Mr. President, in my respectful submission, that should be tendered. The pages filed by the Defence go up to the 25th of January, 1993. It's my submission that all of those pages should be tendered. And in fairness, I should draw it to your attention that there was at the time a dispute as to which pages should be provided and tendered. Mr. President, the particular entry that I have in mind is for the 14th of January, 1993, where there is a reference to the amount of fire coming into the city on the previous night, and there is a reference to that amount of fire being explained by celebration by the Serbs of the Orthodox New Year; in other words, that entry is relevant, in my respectful submission, to the issue, and the issue was whether there was corroboration or at least consistency between the reports generated at the time and the evidence of some witnesses that there was around midnight on certain occasions considerable fire from Bosnian Serb positions into the city. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Defence has -- I haven't got them here at the very moment, but the Defence has filed these parts of annex 6 to the report of the committees of experts. I take it that this is done in order to have them admitted into evidence, all of them. Is that correct, Mr. Piletta-Zanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we could check to see whether these pages are complete, but if I remember correctly I think that your Trial Chamber invited the parties to reduce the number of pages referred to for two months, that is, to do the one that related to December and January, and I think that this is something that we did. I don't know whether we did it by the 25th, because the date of the Serbian New Year is on the 13th of January of each year at the latest, so why go up to the 25th if it's on the 13th? And general you celebrate New Year on the day of the new year and not later. Generally, we celebrate it at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that the Defence filed all these pages; is that correct? So you did it yourself, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. The only question is whether you filed them rather than you tendered them into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I didn't do that myself. Someone from the Defence did that. We provided it to Madam Registrar at the time, I think. I think these documents should be in the hands of Madam Registrar. I think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But I do understand that the documents you filed are the documents you want to tender into -- is that correct? They are in the hands of the -- but the parties were invited to admit this into evidence. Filing is not the same as --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We only complied with an instruction issued by your Trial Chamber in which you requested that the parties provide you with all the relevant pages from that period. All we did was follow your instructions. And it is for you to decide whether this amounts to submitting in evidence, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll deal with that after the break. We'll adjourn and we'll deal with the Radinovic material after the break. But let me just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll adjourn until quarter past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would first like to return to one of the last issues we dealt with before the break, that is, the tendering of the documents the Chamber has asked for. We have asked for the end-of-the-month report of December and of January the senior military observers. We have also asked the -- the relevant part of annex 6 to the report of the committee of experts. And as the Chamber said on the 17th of January, dealing with the period of the 22nd of January until the 8th of January -- so December 1992 until the 8th of January, 1993. Mr. Ierace, you've just told us that you'd like to have it extended beyond the 13th. But before you do that, approximately eight minutes later on that same 17th of January, you asked the same. You said, "We have, in any event, the monthly report" -- no, you said, "Your Honours will see a comment that it's anticipated that there may be activity -- excuse me, I'll go straight to the reference. Yes. I could read out the comment or it's a matter for Your Honours to read it, but it appears on page 4 under the date of the 13th of January." I do the same as everyone. When I read, I go too quickly. You asked previous to that, Mr. Ierace, to have it extended until the 13th or 14th of January. And then you said, "We have, in any event, the monthly report, so I think that's probably sufficient for the 13th of January." Then I said, "So there's no -- you withdraw the extension?" And then your answer was, "Yes." And then I said, "So would then the annexes -- annex 6 should then cover the period of the 22nd of December until the 8th of January." So you've clearly at that moment withdrawn a similar request for extension, Mr. Ierace. Is there anything which differs from what happened on the 17th of January? I mean, I have not printed out the part where you refer to that same -- I think the 13th or 14th of January event described in the year -- in the report of the senior military observers.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, you just said the 17th of January. I think perhaps you meant the 13th or 14th of January.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The -- no, the 17th of January, 2003 was the date on which the matter was discussed, the 17th of this year.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, yes. Yes. I understand now. Mr. President, whilst we deal with the matter of Radinovic, might I be excused to check the contents of the January 1993 report in relation to that date so that I can refresh my memory. At this stage I'd like to keep open --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: -- The opportunity of submitting that we do include the entry for the 14th of January, 1993 from the committee of experts report. I note that the source for the reporting of heavy tank and mortar fire hitting the centre of the city, the heaviest being around midnight and so on, is Reuters, not the senior military observers report or SITREP. So I wish to check that. Could I have that opportunity, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you have that opportunity.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But if you have withdrawn it clearly on the 17th of January, there should be something new in order to reconsider the matter now.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes. That is why I specifically said as a matter of fairness I wanted to alert you to the fact that there was some argument on that date about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Rather to simply let it be tendered without it being drawn to your attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, whilst I'm on my feet, I checked the LiveNote during the break and there was another document that we did not finally settle last Tuesday and that was put over until today, and that is the minutes of the meeting of the 14th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that I mentioned it. Did you then ask, Ms. Pilipovic, to get more time for that? In that case, I failed to reintroduce the matter at this very moment. These are the minutes of the meeting of the municipalities which appear now in a lot of versions, with page 2, without page 2, with two stamps, one stamps. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we didn't have more time to see this, but I believe it's very good that -- it's a very good idea for the Prosecution to refresh their memory. They should take time to do this, because contrary to what Mr. Ierace said, this is not the first time he said he didn't say something. I checked, and the Prosecution is wrong about this. The Prosecution said, 20.900: "My assertion in this first stage is that this segment should be removed from evidence." Mr. President, we talked about the well-known segment that was referred to when I just said that the Defence can actually accept the proposal of the Prosecution, the Prosecutor Ierace said that he never said that. So I'm quoting from page 20.900 of the transcript of the 7th March 2003 to show this. I think it's not nice for somebody to say they never said something when they actually did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just check what exactly. I do remember that Mr. Ierace said that he did not oppose against -- no, that he did not ask for the exclusion of that part, and you say that he did, Mr. Piletta-Zanin; is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just said what Mr. Ierace asserted on the 7th of March, 2003. On page 20.900, he proposed that at the time, I just indicated so, and then he said he never said it, since it is the same person speaking in the same courtroom, I would like to ask him how are we to understand it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's still not -- it's not quite clear what you were quoting. You're referring to a page. But did you quote -- my assertion -- is that the quote, my assertion in this first stage is that this session should be removed from evidence? Is that the quote, Mr. Piletta-Zanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's it, Mr. President. That's it. And when I just said a moment ago that I could accept this proposal of the Prosecution, the Prosecution said they never made the proposal. It's as simple as that. But when I am told something, I think that it either stands or it doesn't stand. In any case, we have to know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm just trying to find the context, Mr. -- You quoted "my assertion in this first stage is." Let me ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe that in view of the hour this issue doesn't really have to be resolved now. We can move on to dealing with other issues, not to waste time. The question was really of the first sequence of this tape. We are talking about two sequences. And the Prosecution doesn't seem to be talking about the same thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I've found it. It's a bit different. It says, "My submission at this stage is, firstly, that the -- that segment be removed from evidence, the transcript in relation to it should remain." So Mr. Ierace wanted the transcript to remain and the videotape be excluded from evidence. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Quite, quite so, Mr. President. But I said a moment ago that I could accept this proposal to withdraw this first sequence of the tape, and when I said this, the Prosecution, which otherwise does not react, say they had never made the proposal, and they did. So I quoted it for you. And this is not the first time. And I'm afraid that this is not the last either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, this last remark did not really assist the Chamber in the task it has to fulfil. Then we have the minutes, because that's where we started, the minutes of the meeting. Could the Defence give its position. Yes, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in its submission of the 21st of February, 2003 the Defence stated its position on the documents presented to Mrs. Jelena Guskova during her testimony so that the document, which is in the form of the minutes of the meeting with the commanders in that area of responsibility. And I think in previous discussion you asked submissions by parties in writing. I believe we did make such a submission. I am not sure about our learned friends from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Has the Prosecution made any submission in writing in respect of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't recall that we did. But that's something I haven't checked. The way it was left on Tuesday was for -- as I understood, it was for oral submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure about that, Mr. Ierace. I would have to check it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What I see in the transcript of last Tuesday, that we dealt with it at five minutes past 7.00, and then we seemed to be in a hurry because I said, "We -- if there's any submission to be made by the Prosecution in respect of that document, but I think there was a response already, but we'll deal with the matter next Friday." So I might have been mistaken that there was already a response. Do you want to respond then orally, if there's no written submission?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the issue, as I understand it, is that we have a translation into the English language which contained a comment presumably by the translator that certain words were double underlined, and we have two copies of the B/C/S document, one of which was double underlined and one which wasn't. My submission is simply that that is not surprising as a matter of common knowledge, the Prosecution obtains documents from different sources, sometimes the same document from different sources. And therefore, it contains more than one ERN number. The important aspect is whether there's any difference in the B/C/S words. In the original document, I don't think it's ever been suggested that there is a difference in the wording. And therefore, Mr. President, the -- if there's no dispute as to the B/C/S contents of the original documents, it doesn't matter that an English translation contains a comment. I don't suggest that comments should be in there. The comment was removed on the last occasion when the document was used in relation to Mr. Radinovic. That's my submission on the matter, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much. The Chamber will give a decision on the admission into evidence of that document. I think that is -- by the way, is one of the Radinovic documents. So therefore, we moved already into our next subject --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, just before you do that fully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The document was also tendered, I think into evidence, through Mr. Donia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I know that. But that was -- that was a different document because that was the same document but without page 2 and not with the same stamps on it, and I think that was the one with the underlining and the other one was not. But we do have one document which very much resembles the document tendered through the witness Radinovic which seems to relate to the same meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll give it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I have a question for Ms. Pilipovic. I'm looking at the document of 21st February regarding this document, as far as I know. Sorry. The last paragraph you make reference to the question of erasing from documentation where Kazani is mentioned," end of the brackets. And I would like to have some explanation on that because I cannot -- I don't remember at this very moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it is a document that the Defence team has received from the Prosecution where I only quoted an example, saying that there was something erased in the document. So I asked the question of what the consequences are when the Defence is being confused. First we received one document, then we received a different document with different numbers with the second page missing. I just made a comparison. If you remember, this is a document that was in colour, it was a photocopy, we used it during examination of a protected witness, I believe. It was just an example of something being erased from a document, of a redaction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: I know the document. I know which is the document. But when you make a reference to Kazani, it's because the second page of that document made a reference to Kazani, the missing page?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: That's what I --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: That's what I don't understand. Which is the reference here?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not the second page.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, if you allow me. It is actually simple. What Mrs. Pilipovic wanted to say is that she thought the method was the same when producing incomplete documents and when producing this document, because the name of Kazani was redacted. Those are the numbers that we will probably never know. It was just a question of making a parallel between two situations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... One document, as far as I remember, it was a list of people killed and wounded and so on, where the word was erased. At that -- it has nothing to do with this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was then a case of what we call the current problem, namely a register, a record kept at the police, an everyday record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That being clarified, I do understand that there's, before we move on to the Radinovic documents, that there's one exhibit that the Defence would like to tender, that's D Exhibit 1914, which is the front page of a lexicon of foreign words published in Belgrade, 1996, and the -- and another -- another dictionary, it seems, which reads "Recnik" and it seems to be, as far as I can see, Serbian-Croatian-French. It says "Srpsko-Hrvatsko-Francuski" and the relevant pages and the pages in the last dictionary I mentioned was the page where the word "strah" appears and in the first lexicon the page on which the word "teror" appears. Is that correct, Mr. President? Is there any objection as to the admission into evidence? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, just to indicate that we have seen this document. The Prosecution wanted to know what the parenthesis meant after the word "teror." For their information, there is a Cyrillic letter "L" which means "Latinic." And "teror" indicated the etymology which is present in all good dictionaries. And just a moment ago I want to correct the English booth. I wasn't talking about a current problem. I was talking about a record at the police where complaints are filed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. An everyday record, as far as I understood. So that is then admitted D1914. Then, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I would like to draw your attention -- but I just have to consult Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, Ms. Pilipovic, D Exhibit 72, which is a videotape, it appears that when it's played it's not very clear, and I would like to give you an opportunity to check with the registry whether this is really what is on the original as well because there might be some confusion. Perhaps it's a bad tape. I do not know. But I just draw your attention to it so that there is an opportunity to --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We should ask Madam Registrar, who knows everything, what the content of this tape is so that we can find this immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was submitted on the 14th of March of this year, so I think on the basis of the transcript you could find out what the context is. But if you could immediately answer that question, Madam Registrar, then ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we could know who the witness was perhaps, that would help us to localise this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... Of last year. I'm making a mistake. It's 14th of March, 2002. And I do understand that it's a tape about the Markale market. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's a tape about the Markale market that has been submitted on the 14th of March of 2002. Then I invited the -- yes, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It was tendered through Witness Sablija on 14/03/02.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then finally we've only ten minutes left, and it might be the wisest thing to do is to give a written decision on the whole discussion on the exhibits that came to us through the witness Radinovic or as an attachment to his report. Ms. Pilipovic, last Tuesday you said that it would be difficult for you to respond right away to the list the Prosecution has given wherein it gives a summary explanation of its view on the Radinovic report but also on Radinovic documents, Radinovic experts. Could you give your response on that document now, or would you prefer to do that in writing or would it be a general response or a very specific response?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that this has been written, but nevertheless it seems that we sent a submission on the 20th with regard to this issue -- but nevertheless, Mr. President, we can say the following: First of all, it's not normal for the Prosecution to have provided us with this list at such a late date because it consists of 16 pages and we refuse to believe that these 16 pages were written on the 18th or 19th. It is obvious that the Prosecution was aware of all the points that it mentioned in detail when the general was here and when the general testified. It's at that point that the Prosecution should have informed us, at least partially, and then the Prosecution should have raised the matter of these problems to provide us with opportunity of responding if necessary. It didn't do that, and we think that this should have been done. On the other hand, General Radinovic clearly said that he had viewed an important -- a significant number of documents. These documents were partially provided to him by the Defence. He immediately recognised them without notes on the basis of his memory, and this shows how well he was acquainted with this matter. And finally, the third point, in order to fully state what our position is with regard to this matter: The Defence thinks that its rights have been in a certain sense violated. Its right to a fair proceedings, a fair judgment, in that the Defence was not in a position to show each document to the witness, each document that Mrs. Pilipovic intended to show the witness. A decision was taken after the Chamber intervened. It was said, "if you carry on in this manner you will have less time granted to you and it will not be extended," and as a result we did not have the time to provide this in order to follow as suggested by your Trial Chamber. And in a certain sense we think that it is bad for the Prosecution to benefit from this. All the documents that were provided to the witness have to be rejected. Why? There were about 200 pages -- this report of the witness refers to a collection of documents, and it functions in relation to this collection of documents. To want to reject these documents is a certain way to reject important documents and also to prejudice the contents, and we can't accept this. The Defence can't accept this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis -- well, first of all, I can establish that after hearing from the Prosecution that the Defence could have taken profit from certain documents provided, but now the balance is restored because the Defence takes that the Prosecution would do better by taking advantage of the documents provided. But apart from that, any other observations?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Just a couple of brief observations, if I may, Mr. President. First of all, it strains credibility for the Defence to argue that they were completely taken by surprise with respect to the 16-page document which we provided. The Prosecution has consistently raised the issue of the methodology used by this expert witness. We have consistently raised the issue that the footnotes, we were unable to find some of the footnotes. It was unclear what some of the materials were referred to in the footnotes. You will recall I made oral submissions to the Trial Chamber before this witness testified raising many of these same issues. The 16-page document which was handed up on Tuesday was initially to be an outline of oral submissions that I would make with respect to the issue of these documents. As I was preparing this list, it became quite obvious that to do so in an oral setting would take far more time than would be worthwhile or far more time than the Trial Chamber reasonably would permit me to do. Shortly before the hearing commenced on Tuesday a decision was taken to simply print out that document and make it available to the Defence and to Your Honours as a simple way of summarising the arguments which the Prosecution anticipated would have taken place on Tuesday during the session that was -- that was held. But again, just as a brief point, Mr. President, the Prosecution has consistently raised this issue. We have been -- there's written correspondence, there have been filings made, there have been a number of occasions where we have raised issues pertaining to the documents and the use thereof by this witness, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That needs no further explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And again, if the Chamber would feel that it's necessary to have this issue more fully briefed, we're prepared to do that in writing. But again, as a basic starting point, I think the Prosecution view with respect to the documents is quite clear from that list that is provided to you. One issue that remains would be the admissibility of the expert report, and again we would object to the admissibility of that report in total for reasons which I could set forth either orally or in writing at the Trial Chamber's convenience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would that bring any specific new elements, compared to what has been submitted previously by the Prosecution in this respect? Because we have had already some submissions on the admissibility or the inadmissibility of the report as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: There would be a couple of -- of newer issues, Mr. President, relating to the testimony of the witness and the sources that he did use, and there would also be some legal argumentation involved with respect to some of the jurisprudence of the Tribunal with respect to expert reports which in the Prosecution view this report has raised a number of issues that have been dealt with by other Trial Chambers and we would be prepared to address the legal arguments with respect to those aspects.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I listened to what my learned colleague said with attention, and I understand what the mechanism desired by the Prosecution was, but that surprises me even more because this is contrary to the principle of the oral nature of the hearing. The Prosecution said that it did this to save time, that is to say, as far as the respect of the parties and the number of hours granted to each party is concerned, the Prosecution by following this procedure provided you with a written document and did exactly the contrary of what the Defence wanted to do in its restricted time; that is to say, it wanted to enter into the substance of the document to be able to prove what the witness knew about it, what he could say about it before you. The Prosecution simply wanted to bypass the principle of the oral nature of the hearings and this is not admissible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for your explanation of the position of the Defence, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. The Chamber suggests that any additional argument to this summary explanation and/or a short explanation of what a summary explanation is- although, it's quite clear. We read that you briefly indicate where the problems are, as far as the Prosecution is concerned, so I wouldn't say that that needs much more explanation. But of course until now it's just a piece of paper to assist us in hearing oral argument. From this piece of paper it appears that this is not a matter which is preferably dealt with orally because it creates a lot of confusion. Therefore, the Prosecution, if they want to keep this document as a -- well, as an itinerary through the report and the annexes and other documents, that this would be filed perhaps as an annex to any additional legal argument, that the Defence responds to that also in writing so that we could deal with the matter. It will take some time because it's -- at least the overwhelming number of documents, not only those attached to the report but also those introduced during the testimony of the witness, is such that we cannot deal with it in five minutes. That's impossible. So the parties are invited to do so. I would expect you, Mr. -- when do you think you could produce that? Because it does not interfere in whatever way, I would say, with the rebuttal evidence. I mean, the rebuttal evidence is limited now to Mr. Tait-Harris, the photograph of the back of the person, which is totally different from this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would anticipate that we would be able to file certainly no later than close of business on Tuesday and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: -- Perhaps close of business on Monday. But to be safe, I would say close of business on Tuesday. We should have no problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if you would do so. And the Defence already has the basic part, that is, the document in its possession so that they could start working on it. And let's -- the Chamber would like to have your response then not later than the end of next week. So that would give you three additional days. And then we'll give a decision on it. At the same time - and I'm now looking forward to next week- can the Chamber expect that Mr. Tait-Harris will be called right on Monday?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, at 9.00 on Monday morning, assuming that the Defence needs to hear from him. Perhaps I should clarify. His statement is 92 bis'ed. Do you wish him to lead evidence in chief that he took the photographs or will his evidence be accepted for the purpose of evidence in chief?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if he would -- that part of his statement is extremely short. Let me just confer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Assuming that the examination of Mr. Tait-Harris would be limited to the issue raised, we leave it up to you whether you want to present him as a 92 bis --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I'm happy with 92 bis, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But then only that part of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, that's understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So that would be -- but if you say it's difficult for us, then -- well, to put, to ask the same questions from him, we'll take -- it will take five minutes. But 92 bis is no problem, as far as the Chamber is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Evidence in chief will be simply a matter of the witness identifying himself. Mr. President, two other issues very quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: In relation to the annex 6, I do seek that that part of January up to and including the entry for the 14th of January be included. It does go beyond what's in the senior military observer's report for the month of January 1993. These were documents called for on the initiative of the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And I think it would be artificial not to include it, since it is clearly relevant. Mr. President, if I might move on to another matter very quickly. Given the finding, the decision of the Trial Chamber earlier this evening, and having regard to an earlier decision as to the timetable to be applied from the time of rebuttal, assuming there is no rejoinder and assuming that that issue is determined, that is, if there is rejoinder, on Monday and that the result is that there is no rejoinder, applying the timetable, that would suggest that written submissions have to be filed by, I think, the -- the 7th of April. And having regard to Rule 86, that would in turn suggest that oral submissions would be either on the 14th or at some stage in that week, which is the week before Easter. It would be of assistance to us, as you might imagine, Mr. President, in planning our human resources if that could be confirmed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I must say I would rather confirm that. I don't know whether you want to arrange for all of it during the weekend. If not, the Chamber would prefer to have a closer look at it and deal with it on Monday, not to make any mistakes in that respect. Because one of the things -- one of your assumptions is - and I'm now turning to the Defence - is that there will be no rejoinder evidence. Of course the limited extent to which the rebuttal evidence is admitted certainly limits the Defence as well. The Defence should, as it was indicated, at the end of the rebuttal evidence indicate immediately what evidence or rejoinder it seeks to present, unless the Defence could express itself already on it now, knowing that the only issue during rebuttal evidence will be one photograph, not even a medical report, but one photograph of a back of a male person. Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Thank you. To hurry is never a good idea. We thought that -- we thought about this question over the weekend, and we're going to concentrate on this matter and think about it. But if I may, I would like to answer Mr. Ierace who linked up a couple of objects very skillfully, and I was not in a position to answer the first issue. May I respond, in spite of the fact that we are running out of time? I will do so very rapidly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You've got one minute, and then I cannot ask the --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Two minutes, that would be enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It would be quite illogical to add after the 13th something that no longer has anything to do with Christmas or the Serbian New Year. I'm talking about the 14th of January. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's clear. We will adjourn until next Monday morning, the same courtroom, 9.00 in the morning.
